Copper Quarterly October 2010 

# Executive Summary 

## Copper flying to a new all-time high 



- **Sentiment was universally bullish** throughout LME week and prices have continued to build on the recovery of the past few months.  Investment inflows into commodities and copper rebounded in September, supported by both fundamental and macroeconomic indicators.  Our forecasts are only marginally different from those we presented on a preliminary basis before LME Week. 



- **Consumption is strong and growth is still centred on Asia** , with good performance from all products (especially electrical and electronics). **Mine output growth has been subdued this year, in the absence of any major new projects and despite limited production disruptions.** Against this backdrop, we now forecast a refined market deficit of around 120,000t this year. 



- 2011 will be another year of modest growth in production due to mine plan revisions, project delays and scrap shortages.  Consumption growth will moderate as restocking abates and, while substitution losses are anticipated in response to high and volatile copper prices, production will still fall short of requirements and the **market deficit will swell to 400,000t** . 



- Prices will remain erratic through 2011 and the draw down in exchange inventories will push the stocks-to-consumption ratios down to the critical lows seen in 2004 and 2005. **We now expect copper prices to reach new highs in 2011.  These elevated and volatile prices are likely to trigger a further round of significant and permanent demand destruction, initially focussed on the scrap consuming brass mills** . 



- Rationing through demand destruction will gather pace in 2012 against a backdrop of elevated prices and chronically low stocks.  The high copper prices of the previous years will encourage substantial increases in mine supply from projects, which will only come to fruition in 2013.  As production growth outstrips consumption in 2013 and 2014 and large surpluses emerge, prices are expected to fall back to a cyclical low, before recovering the following year as the surplus narrows.

For 2010, higher consumption in China and elsewhere means global consumption is 200,000t above levels three months ago. Lower growth rates in 2011-2013, due to demand destruction, leave consumption 550,000t lower by 2013 and 400,000t lower in 2014, compared to July. **Supply** : Mine plan revisions and project delays have resulted in a lowering of our refined production estimate for 2010 by 100,000t compared to previous forecasts. The reduction widens to 450,000t in 2011 and 260,000t in 2012. Higher output from the bunching of delayed mine projects results in refined output being 440,000t higher by 2014. **Prices** : Given a deficit in 2010 and a larger one in 2011, prices have been raised by $350/t for 2010 and $430/t for 2011. Larger surpluses in 2013 and 2014, weigh on prices so by 2014 our forecast is $1,955/t below three months ago. ### Copper price forecasts averaged $2.32/lb for 2010 US¢/lb

Data: Reuters July 2009 Analysts’ Poll © 2010 CRU International Limited confidential #### Copper outshines expectations It is difficult to believe that only a year ago copper prices were trading at the $6,000/t level and projections for copper in 2010 were $3,000/t lower than current price levels. Copper trading up at $8,000/t was certainly not on the horizon nor anticipated by any analyst. Indeed if we look back to the Reuters poll taken in July last year, the price forecasts by the individual analysts offered a median price forecast for 2010 of $5,130/t (232.7¢/lb). Only one estimate out of the 54 put forward started with a seven, $7,000/t (317.5¢/lb). Back then it seemed inconceivable that the copper price would trade above $7,000/t in 2010, but it has outperformed all expectations and is now more than double the lowest projection of $3,460/t (157¢/lb). At the outset of LME week, it became clear that the copper market had turned exceedingly bullish, with prices touted to hit new highs of $13,000/t for 2011. While it is impossible to pick CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly October 2010 Executive Summary 3 a top to this market, sentiment and interest in the realm of commodities remain key contributors to the prospect of higher prices. This was only recently confirmed with the latest data from Barclays which highlighted a strong rebound in investment flows into commodities in September to the t

hird highest ever level of $8.5bn, which pushed commodity assets to an alltime high of $320bn. There is no doubt that higher and more volatile prices are now a key feature of the copper market. Producers are concerned about the impact of these higher prices on their customers and on demand. Consumers are equally, if not more, concerned. At these elevated price levels the cost of working stock escalates and at the same time, profitability and margins suffer. We expect that there will be further substitution losses as a direct result of these higher prices. However, we must note that these will not all be in the refined market in the first instance. When we discuss substitution losses we are referring to losses in the semi manufactured products industry, a market that consumes both scrap and refined and which we estimated to be around 23Mt in 2009 (17Mt refined and 6Mt scrap). Our analysis of copper substitution suggests that losses in the copper industry could amount to 300,000 tonnes in 2010 and 450,000-460,000 tonnes in 2011 and 2012 based on previous extensive work that has been carried out. We also understand that not all these losses are going to aluminium as there are applications where plastics will win share away from copper. Although consumers have been here before, there is an increased risk of higher and larger substitution losses the longer prices remain high and volatile relative to the substitutes for copper. Based on the current and forecast prices, the ratio of copper to aluminium is already significantly above the critical 3 to 1 level. In 2010, latest estimates suggest an outturn of 3.4 to 1, rising to 3.6 to 1 in 2011. However, analysts’ forecasts are all but exact. The magnitude and timing of future substitution losses is an inexact science and a major area of uncertainty. Cu / Al price differential and price ratio

CRU International Limited confidential 4 Copper Quarterly October 2010 Executive Summary At the current price differential between aluminium and copper, consumers are in a difficult position and faced with tough decisions; do the producers of the end-use products that consume copper take the plunge and invest in R&D and then take on the additional cost of re-tooling etc. to use aluminium or other substitutes? Not only must end-users bear this additional cost, but they must also understand if there are any capacity constrain

ts on the substitutes.  We know from previous analysis of substitution losses that once the switch is made, it is lost for good (practically speaking).  A mounting concern with prices trading at the current levels is that now, copper usage in any new high growth applications could potentially be ruled out from the outset. 

#### Production is the key 

These next couple of years could therefore prove to be very critical for copper – will supply respond quickly enough to avoid more widespread substitution?  On the face of it, we still see a concentrates market that is forecast to remain tight for the outlook period.  There is an excess of smelting capacity, the majority of which is located in China as the country continues to feed its need for industrial raw materials and refined copper in particular.  What is key as we look ahead is that refined production will benefit both from the rise of concentrate and EW cathode output from the swathe of projects that are due to come through over the next few years, as well as higher secondary production.  The recent upward trend of copper prices, combined with bullish expectations for the following years, has set the scene for promising news about project developments.  2013 is a pivotal year with a sizeable addition to production of 1.24Mt from firm projects alone (a full list of mine projects is in Appendix C.2).  Output from these projects alongside the copper producers’ ability to buy scrap, at a cost to the brass mill sector, will support solid refined production growth in the 2012-2014 timeframe.

Between 2010 and 2012, new mine production will come from brownfield projects such as Andina, Los Pelambres and Los Bronces, as producers can take advantage of previous or operating facilities. In 2013, we expect to see more production coming from greenfield projects – in particular Oyu Tolgoi. In recent months, announcements about projects going ahead include: Xstrata for Las Bambas (Peru) and PanAust for an expansion at Phu Kham (Laos). Other developments include several projects approving feasibility studies, handing in their Environmental Impact Study and increasing reserves and resources. Among the latter, Anglo American and Xstrata announced maiden resources at their West Wall project, which is c

lose to their Los Bronces mine (Chile). In addition, Vale and African Rainbow Minerals broke ground at their joint venture project Konkola North (Zambia), and Xstrata announced the start of construction at Antapaccay (Peru). CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly October 2010 Executive Summary 7 As production from projects and new mines comes through, annual mine supply growth will rise to a peak of 6.5% in 2013. Nevertheless, miners will remain in a strong position reflecting the consistently tight concentrate market, which will be due mainly to Chinese smelter expansions. As a result, TC/RCs will remain low throughout the outlook period. Strong growth in scrap usage by smelters and refineries (as scrap is diverted from semi fabricators) will underpin a consistently higher growth rate of refined output relative to mine supply. #### Consumption strong but facing demand destruction threat Despite the escalating fear about potential substitution losses, consumption has been exceptionally strong this year. The Asian-centric recovery from 2009 has continued through 2010. Growth in North America and Western Europe is lagging the world average, and there are now no longer any fears of an imminent double dip recession. We estimate that world refined copper consumption will rise by 8.4% to 18.5Mt in 2010, more than offsetting the contraction in 2009. The biggest contributor remains China, which is expected to account for 38% of the world market in 2010. The recovery in demand is being driven by the automotive, domestic appliance and electrical and electronic sectors. Production of flat rolled products outperformed all other semis in H1 2010, supported by robust demand from electrical and electronic applications. In 2010 and 2

011 we see synchronised growth across all regions for both refined copper and in the wire and cable sector.  The last time this occurred was in 2004, the last trigger for copper prices to escalate. 

According to our projections, the refined copper market will exhibit above average growth rates in all but one of the years over the period 2012-2015.  We believe that future demand growth will be mainly driven by copper’s superior electrical conductivity.  This is backed and justified by the new capacity in wirerod and flat rolled products.  Only high value added products will continue to use copper, especially at the current price level. 

As we highlighted earlier, higher and volatile prices will lead to the onset of a round of significant and permanent demand destruction (rationing in mainly non-electrical applications). Scrap is already being rationed as copper producers outbid the brass mills. The innovative micro channel technology is also a strong competitive threat to conventional designs and continues to make inroads in the US.  This new technology also ensures that high SEER requirements (Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio) are met, so the key issue is when new standards will be introduced, as this wi

ll further drive the switch to all aluminium designs. #### Scrap shortages to continue, supporting refined demand Scrap has now become a very important component of the copper market. After the crash in copper prices in Q4 2008, following the turmoil in financial markets, scrap had all but disappeared as economic activity stalled. 2009 was a year of very poor scrap generation and availability. Moreover, we believe that there is no longer a readily available scrap pool for the copper market to draw on and users are dependent on current generation. Also, given that industrial production remains well below peak levels in the major scrap markets of North America and Western Europe, lower quantities of process scrap are being generated. The global supply of scrap (using world copper scrap trade as a proxy) remains over 20% below pre-crisis levels. The impact of the tightness is being felt almost entirely in China and partly explains the escalation in refined consumption growth last year, as cathode imports made up the shortfall. Higher copper prices and low scrap discounts have seen smelters outbidding semi fabricators to buy the scrap that is available. Copper’s superior electrical conductivity

CRU International Limited confidential 10 Copper Quarterly October 2010 Executive Summary #### Deficits to push stocks down to critical levels The combination of higher consumption and flat production growth alongside limited scrap availability has seen exchange stocks run down by a third from their peaks in February 2010. This has brought the exchange stock-to-consumption ratio down to the level of a year ago of around 1.5 weeks, similar to that at the end of the Chinese import boom. The combination of lower refined output with slowing but still strong consumption growth in 2011 means that the market deficit will expand to 420,000t next year. The tight market in 2011 will also push stockto-consumption ratios down to the historic lows last seen in 2004-2005 (0.4-0.5 weeks), where they will remain in 2012. Moderating refined consumption growth, as the effects of rationing due to the high prices come into play, will lead to substantial surpluses emerging in the refined market and a build in exchange inventories. Copper prices will surrender to the large surpluses easing to a cyclical low of $6,900/t ($3.13/lb) in 2014. By 2015, however, growth in mine supply will lag that of demand and we anticipate that the large surplus will be eroded slightly. Prices will once again start to tick up to average $7,100/t ($3.22/lb) ahead of tighter market conditions in the years ahead. Investment money has been an important factor in the recovery in prices, with the copper component of the GSCI and DJ-UBS indices alone between October and July rising by 18% and accounting for the investment equivalent of over 600,000t of copper. The recovery in market sentiment will only fuel the further rise in allocations to commodities, including copper. The dollar depreciation to over $1.30/€ has also helped push prices back above $8,000/t. However, CRU’s dollar forecasts mean that the currency effect will be a relatively benign influence on prices over the outlook period. Nevertheless, we expect to see investment allocations to continue to support prices in the next couple of years. |Table V: World copper s
